ionic.tagline: Electrons transfer completely, forming oppositely charged ions that attract each other.
ionic.formation: When atoms with very different electronegativities meet, the less electronegative atom transfers an electron completely to the more electronegative atom, forming a positive and a negative ion.
ionic.electronBehavior: Electrons move from the metal atom (e.g. sodium) completely to the nonmetal atom (e.g. chlorine) — a one-way, complete transfer with no shared electron pair.
ionic.characteristics: The bond forms through electrostatic attraction (Coulomb force) between oppositely charged ions. Ionic compounds typically have high melting and boiling points, and conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, not as a solid.
ionic.typicalExamples: Sodium chloride (NaCl), magnesium oxide (MgO), potassium chloride (KCl).
ionic.commonSubstances: Table salt, most alkali metal halides, many mineral crystals.
ionic.realWorldUses: Table salt is used for seasoning and food preservation; ionic compounds are widely used in electrolyte solutions, fertilizers, and industrial materials.
ionic.misconceptions: A common misconception is that electron transfer in an ionic bond happens gradually — once an ionic bond forms, the electron fully belongs to the receiving atom, with no "partially transferred" intermediate state (that's what happens in a polar covalent bond).

covalent.tagline: Two atoms share one or more electron pairs; electronegativities are similar or equal.
covalent.formation: When two atoms have similar or identical electronegativities, they achieve a stable electron configuration by sharing one or more electron pairs instead of transferring electrons.
covalent.electronBehavior: The shared electron pair is attracted equally by both nuclei, distributed evenly between them rather than favoring either atom.
covalent.characteristics: The bond is directional, and bond strength varies with bond order (single, double, triple); nonpolar covalent molecules typically have lower melting/boiling points and don't conduct electricity as solids.
covalent.commonSubstances: Atmospheric O₂ and N₂; methane, the main component of natural gas; dry ice (solid CO₂).
covalent.realWorldUses: Methane is the primary fuel component of natural gas; carbon dioxide is used in carbonated drinks and fire extinguishers; chlorine gas is used to disinfect water.
covalent.misconceptions: A common misconception is that all covalent bonds are "weak and non-conducting" — in fact covalent bonds can be extremely strong (like the carbon–carbon bonds in diamond); a covalent substance's physical properties depend on molecular structure and intermolecular forces, not the bond type itself.

polarCovalent.tagline: The electron pair is shared, but shifted toward one atom due to an electronegativity difference.
polarCovalent.formation: When two bonded atoms have a moderate electronegativity difference (roughly 0.4–1.7), the electron pair is still shared, but shifts toward the more electronegative atom, creating partial charges.
polarCovalent.electronBehavior: The shared electron pair's density shifts toward the more electronegative atom (e.g. Cl in HCl), giving it a partial negative charge (δ⁻) while the other atom carries a partial positive charge (δ⁺).
polarCovalent.characteristics: Depending on bond polarity and molecular shape, a molecule may have a net dipole moment, making the whole molecule polar and affecting boiling point, solubility, and intermolecular forces.
polarCovalent.commonSubstances: Water; ammonia solution; hydrochloric acid (aqueous HCl).
polarCovalent.realWorldUses: Water's polarity makes it an excellent solvent for ionic and polar substances; ammonia is used in cleaning products and fertilizer production.
polarCovalent.misconceptions: A common misconception is equating "bond polarity" with "molecular polarity" — for example, each C=O bond in CO₂ is polar, but because the molecule is linear, the two bond dipoles cancel out, making the overall molecule nonpolar.

metallic.tagline: Metal cations arranged in a lattice, surrounded by a freely moving "sea" of outer electrons.
metallic.formation: A metal atom's valence electrons don't belong to any single atom — they detach and move freely throughout the entire metallic lattice, leaving behind a regular arrangement of metal cations.
metallic.electronBehavior: The delocalized valence electrons surround all the cations like a "sea of electrons," free to move and carry energy and charge without belonging to any single atom.
metallic.characteristics: The bond has no fixed direction, so the lattice can slide under stress without breaking (giving metals ductility and malleability); the free electrons give metals excellent electrical and thermal conductivity.
metallic.typicalExamples: Iron (Fe), copper (Cu), aluminum (Al), gold (Au), and their alloys.
metallic.commonSubstances: Steel used in construction, copper in electrical wiring, aluminum in beverage cans, gold in jewelry.
metallic.realWorldUses: Copper wire is used for power transmission; aluminum alloys are used in aerospace and vehicles; iron and steel are foundational materials in construction and manufacturing.
metallic.misconceptions: A common misconception is imagining metallic bonding as many separate "atom-to-atom" bonds — it's actually a collective phenomenon where every atom in the metal shares the same sea of free electrons, which can't really be described by a single discrete bond.

hydrogen.tagline: A stronger intermolecular force between hydrogen and a highly electronegative atom (O, N, or F).
hydrogen.formation: When a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (like oxygen, nitrogen, or fluorine), it carries a significant partial positive charge, which is then attracted to a lone pair on a highly electronegative atom in a neighboring molecule, forming a hydrogen bond.
hydrogen.electronBehavior: The hydrogen atom loses most of its electron density to the highly electronegative atom it's covalently bonded to, carrying a partial positive charge (δ⁺); a nearby molecule's electronegative atom attracts this hydrogen with its lone pair.
hydrogen.characteristics: Hydrogen bonds are intermolecular forces, much weaker than covalent or ionic bonds, but noticeably stronger than typical van der Waals forces — strong enough to significantly raise a substance's melting and boiling points.
hydrogen.typicalExamples: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules, between DNA base pairs, and within protein secondary structure.
hydrogen.commonSubstances: Water, ammonia, hydrofluoric acid (HF), ethanol, and other substances with O–H or N–H bonds.
hydrogen.realWorldUses: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules give water its unusually high boiling point and make ice less dense than liquid water (so ice floats); hydrogen bonds also hold DNA's double helix and protein folding structures stable.
hydrogen.misconceptions: A common misconception is treating a hydrogen bond as a "true chemical bond" — it's actually a stronger-than-usual electrostatic attraction between (or within) molecules, not a bond formed by sharing or transferring electrons between atoms.

q1.question: Which statement correctly describes how an ionic bond forms?
options: An electron transfers completely from one atom to another
Electrons move freely throughout a lattice
No electrons are involved in the bond
q1.explanation: The defining feature of an ionic bond is complete electron transfer, not sharing — unlike a covalent bond.

q2.question: In NaCl, which atom attracts electrons more strongly, becoming the negative ion?
q2.explanation: Chlorine's electronegativity (3.16) is far higher than sodium's (0.93), so sodium transfers its electron to chlorine, forming Cl⁻.

q1.question: What type of bond exists in an H₂ molecule?
q1.explanation: Both hydrogen atoms have identical electronegativity, so the electron pair is shared equally — a nonpolar covalent bond.

q2.question: What is the most accurate description of electron behavior in a covalent bond?
options: Electrons transfer completely from one atom to another
Electrons move freely throughout a lattice
Electrons are shared between two atoms
Electrons don't participate in the bond at all
q2.explanation: A covalent bond is defined by atoms sharing an electron pair, not transferring or delocalizing it.

q1.question: In an HCl molecule, which end carries a partial negative charge (δ⁻)?
q1.explanation: Chlorine's higher electronegativity pulls the shared electron pair toward itself, giving it δ⁻ while hydrogen carries δ⁺.

q2.question: Why does HCl form a polar covalent bond instead of an ionic bond?
options: The electronegativity difference between H and Cl falls between 0.4 and 1.7
H and Cl have identical electronegativity
The electron transfers completely to Cl
There's no shared electron pair in this bond
q2.explanation: A moderate electronegativity difference means electrons are shared but unevenly — a larger difference would form an ionic bond instead.

q1.question: How do valence electrons behave in a metallic bond?
options: Fixed in place between two atoms
Move freely throughout the metallic lattice, forming a "sea of electrons"
q1.explanation: Metallic bonding delocalizes valence electrons into a freely moving electron sea — which is also why metals conduct electricity.

q2.question: Which metal property does the "electron sea" model explain?
q2.explanation: Freely moving electrons can carry charge quickly through the metal, giving it good conductivity; metals are typically ductile rather than brittle.

q1.question: A hydrogen bond mainly forms between a hydrogen atom and which kind of atom?
options: A highly electronegative atom, such as O, N, or F
q1.explanation: Hydrogen bonding requires a strongly polar O–H, N–H, or F–H bond as a prerequisite.

q2.question: Compared to a covalent bond, how strong is a hydrogen bond?
options: Far stronger than a covalent bond
Weaker than a covalent bond — it's an intermolecular force
q2.explanation: A hydrogen bond is an intermolecular force — stronger than typical van der Waals forces, but still much weaker than a covalent or ionic bond.

h2o.commonUses: The universal solvent, essential for life, and used for industrial cooling and steam power.
h2o.safetyNotes: Safe for everyday drinking and contact — one of the safest chemical substances there is.
h2o.funFact: Hydrogen bonding between molecules gives water an unusually high boiling point, and makes solid ice less dense than liquid water — which is why ice floats.

co2.commonUses: The raw material for photosynthesis, the fizz in carbonated drinks, and a fire-extinguishing agent.
co2.safetyNotes: Harmless at low concentrations, but can cause oxygen displacement in enclosed spaces at high concentration — ventilation is important.
co2.funFact: Solid carbon dioxide is called dry ice — it sublimates directly into gas at normal pressure without ever becoming liquid.

o2.commonUses: Essential for respiration in living things, required for combustion, and used as medical oxygen.
o2.safetyNotes: Non-toxic itself, but high concentrations significantly increase the fire risk of combustible materials.
o2.funFact: Oxygen makes up about 21% of Earth's atmosphere, almost all of it produced by photosynthesis in plants and algae.

n2.commonUses: An inert protective gas for food packaging, liquid nitrogen for cryogenic storage, and the raw material for ammonia synthesis.
n2.safetyNotes: Chemically stable and non-toxic, but can displace oxygen in enclosed spaces at high concentration.
n2.funFact: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere; its triple bond makes it exceptionally stable and unreactive.

h2.commonUses: Fuel cell energy, the raw material for ammonia synthesis (the Haber process), and rocket fuel.
h2.safetyNotes: Highly flammable with a wide flammability range when mixed with air — avoid open flames and static electricity.
h2.funFact: Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe, making up the vast majority of known matter.

nacl.commonUses: Everyday table salt, food preservation and curing, and de-icing roads.
nacl.safetyNotes: Safe to eat, though excessive intake and prolonged contact with concentrated brine are worth noting.
nacl.funFact: Solid sodium chloride forms a regular cubic crystal lattice, with each ion surrounded by 6 oppositely charged neighbors.

hcl.commonUses: The main component of human stomach acid, an industrial cleaning agent, and a raw material for PVC and other plastics.
hcl.safetyNotes: Corrosive and irritating — the gas or concentrated solution should be handled in a well-ventilated environment.
hcl.funFact: Your stomach secretes hydrochloric acid (aqueous HCl) at a pH as low as 1–2 to help digest food.

nh3.commonUses: The main raw material for fertilizer production, cleaning products, and an industrial refrigerant.
nh3.safetyNotes: Pungent and corrosive — inhaling high concentrations irritates the respiratory tract; requires ventilation.
nh3.funFact: Even though it's a gas at room temperature, ammonia is extremely soluble in water thanks to hydrogen bonding — one volume of water can dissolve over a hundred times its volume in ammonia gas.

ch4.commonUses: The main component of natural gas and household fuel, and an industrial synthesis feedstock.
ch4.safetyNotes: Colorless, odorless, and highly flammable — leaks require special attention to ignition sources and ventilation.
ch4.funFact: Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and a potent greenhouse gas, commonly produced in landfills and during digestion in ruminant animals.

methanol.commonUses: An industrial solvent, a biofuel additive, and a raw material for organic synthesis.
methanol.safetyNotes: Toxic — accidental ingestion can damage the optic nerve or even be fatal. Industrial use only; never a food substitute.
methanol.funFact: Methanol is the simplest alcohol, differing from methane by just one oxygen atom, yet with drastically different properties.

ethanol.commonUses: Alcoholic beverages, hand sanitizer, a gasoline additive (gasohol), and an industrial solvent.
ethanol.safetyNotes: Relatively safe in moderate amounts when consumed, but highly flammable at high concentration — never to be confused with methanol.
ethanol.funFact: Ethanol is produced by yeast fermenting sugars — a process humans have used for thousands of years.

aceticAcid.commonUses: The main component of vinegar (about 4–8% concentration), a food preservative, and an industrial solvent.
aceticAcid.safetyNotes: Diluted table vinegar is safe, but concentrated pure acetic acid is corrosive and irritates skin and mucous membranes.
aceticAcid.funFact: Pure acetic acid freezes into ice-like crystals below 16.6°C, which is why it's nicknamed "glacial acetic acid."

acetone.commonUses: Nail polish remover, an industrial solvent, and paint thinner.
acetone.safetyNotes: Flammable and volatile — use in a ventilated environment and avoid prolonged inhalation.
acetone.funFact: The human body naturally produces small amounts of acetone during fat metabolism (ketosis), contributing to a distinctive breath odor in ketosis.

benzene.commonUses: A precursor in the chemical industry for synthesizing plastics and detergents; historically also used as a solvent.
benzene.safetyNotes: A known carcinogen — modern use is tightly regulated and requires professional protective equipment and ventilation.
benzene.funFact: Benzene's ring structure was proposed by Kekulé in 1865, reportedly after he dreamed of a snake biting its own tail.

acetaldehyde.commonUses: An intermediate raw material in manufacturing chemicals such as acetic acid.
acetaldehyde.safetyNotes: Irritating and potentially toxic — the body also produces acetaldehyde when metabolizing alcohol, contributing to hangover symptoms.
acetaldehyde.funFact: When the liver breaks down ethanol, it first produces acetaldehyde as an intermediate — its buildup is a major cause of hangover symptoms.

methylAcetate.commonUses: A low-volatility organic solvent used in some paints, adhesives, and nail products.
methylAcetate.safetyNotes: Volatile — prolonged inhalation of vapors may cause discomfort; use in a ventilated environment.
methylAcetate.funFact: Methyl acetate has a fruity odor and occurs naturally in some fruits.

ethylene.commonUses: The raw material for polyethylene plastic, and a plant hormone used agriculturally to ripen fruit.
ethylene.safetyNotes: A flammable gas — industrial handling requires attention to ignition sources and leaks.
ethylene.funFact: Bananas release ethylene gas, which is why storing them with other fruit makes that fruit ripen faster.

acetylene.commonUses: The fuel gas for oxy-acetylene welding and metal cutting, and a chemical synthesis feedstock.
acetylene.safetyNotes: Highly flammable and unstable — high-pressure storage requires special care; burns at temperatures up to about 3300°C.
acetylene.funFact: Acetylene produces one of the hottest flames of any common fuel gas, which is why it's widely used for cutting metal.

methylamine.commonUses: An intermediate raw material in pharmaceutical and agrochemical synthesis.
methylamine.safetyNotes: Pungent and corrosive — requires a ventilated environment to handle.
methylamine.funFact: Methylamine has an ammonia-like, fishy odor and is the simplest primary amine.

acetamide.commonUses: An intermediate in organic synthesis, and a raw material for some industrial solvents and plasticizers.
acetamide.safetyNotes: As with most pure chemicals, handle in a ventilated environment and avoid prolonged contact.
acetamide.funFact: Acetamide can be thought of as acetic acid and ammonia joined with the loss of a water molecule — a representative molecule of the amide functional group.

dimethylEther.commonUses: An aerosol spray propellant, an alternative fuel to LPG, and an organic synthesis solvent.
dimethylEther.safetyNotes: A flammable gas — keep away from open flames; use and store in a ventilated environment.
dimethylEther.funFact: Dimethyl ether and ethanol share the exact same molecular formula, C₂H₆O — they're structural isomers, yet ethanol is a liquid while dimethyl ether is a gas at room temperature and pressure.

organicChemistry.pageSubtitle: Explore organic chemistry as a connected system — from functional groups to molecules, properties, and reactions.

actions.selectSecond: Select a second functional group to compare

alkane.generalStructure: CnH2n+2 — saturated chain or ring compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen.
alkane.characteristicAtoms: Carbon (C) and hydrogen (H), with every carbon fully saturated by single bonds.
alkane.bondPattern: Carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen single bonds only — no functional group, low reactivity.
alkane.keyProperties: Nonpolar, less dense than water, melting/boiling points rise with chain length, chemically fairly inert.
alkane.commonReactions: Combustion (producing CO₂ and water), halogenation (free-radical substitution).

alkene.generalStructure: An unsaturated hydrocarbon with at least one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C).
alkene.characteristicAtoms: Carbon (C) and hydrogen (H); the double-bonded carbons are trigonal planar.
alkene.bondPattern: One σ bond plus one π bond forming the C=C double bond — the π electron cloud is reactive.
alkene.keyProperties: Nonpolar, more reactive than an alkane of the same carbon count; the double bond can undergo addition.
alkene.commonReactions: Addition reactions (with H₂, H₂O, halogens), polymerization.

alkyne.generalStructure: An unsaturated hydrocarbon with at least one carbon-carbon triple bond (C≡C).
alkyne.characteristicAtoms: Carbon (C) and hydrogen (H); the triple-bonded carbons are linear.
alkyne.bondPattern: One σ bond plus two π bonds forming the C≡C triple bond — the shortest, strongest carbon-carbon bond.
alkyne.keyProperties: Nonpolar, more reactive than alkenes; burns at extremely high flame temperatures.
alkyne.commonReactions: Addition reactions (can proceed in two stages), oxy-acetylene combustion.

aromatic.generalStructure: Represented by the benzene ring — a cyclic, conjugated π-electron system with distinctive stability.
aromatic.characteristicAtoms: Carbon (C) and hydrogen (H) forming a ring skeleton with delocalized electrons.
aromatic.bondPattern: Delocalized bonding between single and double bond character, often simplified as alternating single/double bonds (a Kekulé structure).
aromatic.keyProperties: Nonpolar, chemically stable, resists addition reactions in favor of substitution.

alcohol.generalStructure: R-OH — a carbon chain or ring bearing a hydroxyl group.
alcohol.characteristicAtoms: A hydroxyl group made of oxygen (O) and hydrogen (H), attached to the carbon skeleton.
alcohol.bondPattern: Polar C-O and O-H single bonds, with the oxygen carrying a partial negative charge.
alcohol.keyProperties: Polar, hydrogen-bonds with water — small alcohols are water-soluble with higher boiling points than the corresponding alkane.
alcohol.commonReactions: Oxidation (to aldehyde or ketone), esterification (with a carboxylic acid), dehydration condensation (to an ether or alkene).

ether.generalStructure: R-O-R' — two carbon groups linked through an oxygen atom.
ether.characteristicAtoms: An oxygen (O) forming two single bonds to carbon groups on either side; no hydroxyl group.
ether.bondPattern: Two polar C-O single bonds; the oxygen still carries a partial negative charge, but overall reactivity is lower than an alcohol's.
ether.keyProperties: Weakly polar, chemically fairly stable and resistant to oxidation — commonly used as a solvent in organic reactions.
ether.commonReactions: Low reactivity, mainly used as a solvent; the ether bond can cleave under strong acid.

aldehyde.generalStructure: R-CHO — a carbonyl and a hydrogen at the end of a carbon chain.
aldehyde.characteristicAtoms: A carbon-oxygen double bond (C=O) with a hydrogen directly attached.
aldehyde.bondPattern: A polar carbon-oxygen double bond; the carbon is trigonal planar, the oxygen carries a partial negative charge.
aldehyde.keyProperties: Polar, boiling point higher than the corresponding alkane but lower than an alcohol; the carbonyl makes it easily oxidized.
aldehyde.commonReactions: Oxidation (to a carboxylic acid), reduction (to an alcohol), addition with an alcohol to form a hemiacetal.

ketone.generalStructure: R-CO-R' — a carbonyl flanked by carbon groups on both sides.
ketone.characteristicAtoms: A carbon-oxygen double bond (C=O) with carbon, not hydrogen, on both sides.
ketone.bondPattern: A polar carbon-oxygen double bond; the carbon is trigonal planar.
ketone.keyProperties: Polar, chemically more stable than an aldehyde and resistant to further oxidation.
ketone.commonReactions: Reduction (to a secondary alcohol), addition with an alcohol to form a ketal.

carboxylicAcid.generalStructure: R-COOH — a carboxyl group at the end of a carbon chain.
carboxylicAcid.characteristicAtoms: A carbonyl (C=O) and a hydroxyl (-OH) together forming the carboxyl group.
carboxylicAcid.bondPattern: A carbon-oxygen double bond alongside a carbon-oxygen single bond; distinctly acidic, releasing H⁺.
carboxylicAcid.keyProperties: Polar and acidic — neutralizes with base to form a salt; small carboxylic acids are water-soluble.
carboxylicAcid.commonReactions: Esterification (with an alcohol to form an ester), neutralization (with base to form a salt), amidation (with an amine to form an amide).

ester.generalStructure: R-COO-R' — the condensation product of a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
ester.characteristicAtoms: A carbonyl (C=O) and an ester-linkage oxygen connecting two carbon groups.
ester.bondPattern: A polar carbon-oxygen double bond alongside a single bond, but without acidity.
ester.keyProperties: Polar, often has a distinctive fruity smell, chemically milder than the parent carboxylic acid.
ester.commonReactions: Hydrolysis (to a carboxylic acid and an alcohol), saponification (base hydrolysis to a salt and an alcohol).

amine.generalStructure: R-NH₂ (or R₂NH, R₃N) — a carbon chain bearing an amino group.
amine.characteristicAtoms: A nitrogen (N) carrying a lone pair, bonded to one to three carbon groups.
amine.bondPattern: Polar C-N and N-H single bonds; the nitrogen's lone pair gives it basic character.
amine.keyProperties: Polar and basic — small amines often have a fishy smell and form ammonium salts with acids.
amine.commonReactions: Neutralization with acid (to an ammonium salt), amidation with a carboxylic acid.

amide.generalStructure: R-CO-NH₂ — the condensation product of a carboxylic acid and an amine.
amide.characteristicAtoms: A carbonyl (C=O) directly bonded to an amino nitrogen (N).
amide.bondPattern: A carbon-oxygen double bond alongside a carbon-nitrogen single bond — the basis of the peptide bond in proteins.
amide.keyProperties: Polar, chemically stable, neither notably acidic nor basic.
amide.commonReactions: Hydrolysis (breaking down to a carboxylic acid and an amine under acid or base).

labels.symbolicOxidantNote: "[O]" represents the net oxidizing effect supplied by the oxidizing agent — a common textbook shorthand, not an actual molecule.

combustionMethane.name: Combustion of Methane
combustionMethane.summary: Methane burns completely in excess oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of heat — the chemical basis of natural gas as a fuel.
combustionMethane.whatChanges: Carbon-hydrogen bonds and the oxygen-oxygen bond break; new carbon-oxygen double bonds (in carbon dioxide) and oxygen-hydrogen bonds (in water) form in their place.
combustionMethane.keyTakeaway: The general pattern "hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water" is one of the most characteristic reactions of alkanes.

hydrogenationAcetyleneToEthylene.name: Hydrogenation of Acetylene to Ethylene
hydrogenationAcetyleneToEthylene.summary: With a Lindlar catalyst (a partially poisoned palladium catalyst), acetylene adds only one equivalent of hydrogen and stops at the alkene stage instead of continuing to the alkane.
hydrogenationAcetyleneToEthylene.whatChanges: One π bond of the carbon-carbon triple bond (C≡C) opens, becoming a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C); each carbon gains one additional hydrogen.
hydrogenationAcetyleneToEthylene.keyTakeaway: Choosing a Lindlar catalyst is the key to controlling exactly where a hydrogenation stops — a classic example of precise control in organic synthesis.

hydrogenationEthyleneToEthane.name: Hydrogenation of Ethylene to Ethane
hydrogenationEthyleneToEthane.summary: Ethylene adsorbs hydrogen gas on the surface of a metal catalyst such as nickel, platinum, or palladium, completing an addition reaction that yields saturated ethane.
hydrogenationEthyleneToEthane.whatChanges: The carbon-carbon double bond (C=C) opens into a single bond; each carbon gains one additional hydrogen, becoming a fully saturated alkane.
hydrogenationEthyleneToEthane.keyTakeaway: This is the final step of the alkyne-to-alkane hydrogenation chain, showing how unsaturation drops step by step with each addition.

additionEthyleneToEthanol.name: Hydration of Ethylene to Ethanol
additionEthyleneToEthanol.summary: Ethylene adds water under acid catalysis (such as phosphoric acid) — one of the main industrial routes for producing ethanol at scale.
additionEthyleneToEthanol.whatChanges: The carbon-carbon double bond opens, and one carbon forms a new carbon-oxygen single bond with water's oxygen, producing ethanol's hydroxyl group.
additionEthyleneToEthanol.keyTakeaway: Hydration is a key application of alkene addition reactions, converting a nonpolar hydrocarbon directly into a polar molecule bearing a functional group.

oxidationEthanolToAcetaldehyde.name: Oxidation of Ethanol to Acetaldehyde
oxidationEthanolToAcetaldehyde.summary: Ethanol is mildly oxidized by an oxidizing agent such as acidified potassium dichromate, losing the hydroxyl hydrogen and a carbon-bound hydrogen to form acetaldehyde.
oxidationEthanolToAcetaldehyde.whatChanges: The oxygen-hydrogen bond of the hydroxyl group breaks, along with a carbon-hydrogen bond on the same carbon, forming a new carbon-oxygen double bond (the carbonyl).
oxidationEthanolToAcetaldehyde.keyTakeaway: Oxidizing a primary alcohol yields an aldehyde — a classic example of using oxidant strength to control whether the product stops at the aldehyde or continues to the carboxylic acid.

oxidationAcetaldehydeToAceticAcid.name: Oxidation of Acetaldehyde to Acetic Acid
oxidationAcetaldehydeToAceticAcid.summary: Acetaldehyde's aldehyde group is readily oxidized further; a stronger oxidizing agent such as acidified potassium permanganate fully oxidizes it to acetic acid.
oxidationAcetaldehydeToAceticAcid.whatChanges: The carbon-hydrogen bond on the aldehyde carbon breaks, and an oxygen atom supplied by the oxidant is incorporated, forming the new carbon-oxygen single bond of the carboxyl group.
oxidationAcetaldehydeToAceticAcid.keyTakeaway: Aldehydes oxidize more readily than ketones precisely because the aldehyde carbon still carries a replaceable carbon-hydrogen bond.

condensationMethanolToEther.name: Condensation of Methanol to Dimethyl Ether
condensationMethanolToEther.summary: Two methanol molecules undergo intermolecular dehydration under concentrated sulfuric acid catalysis and heat, forming an ether and water.
condensationMethanolToEther.whatChanges: The oxygen-hydrogen bond of one methanol and the carbon-oxygen bond of the other break and recombine, forming a new ether linkage (C-O-C) and releasing one water molecule.
condensationMethanolToEther.keyTakeaway: Intermolecular dehydration of alcohols is the key route to symmetric ethers — a different direction of dehydration from the intramolecular route that yields alkenes.

esterificationAceticAcidMethanol.name: Esterification of Acetic Acid and Methanol
esterificationAceticAcidMethanol.summary: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol undergo esterification under concentrated sulfuric acid catalysis and reflux — a reversible reaction that produces a fruity-smelling ester.
esterificationAceticAcidMethanol.whatChanges: A carbon-oxygen bond of the carboxylic acid and the oxygen-hydrogen bond of the alcohol break and recombine, forming a new ester linkage (-COO-) and releasing one water molecule.
esterificationAceticAcidMethanol.keyTakeaway: Esterification is reversible — its reverse reaction is ester hydrolysis; the two form a matched equilibrium pair.

hydrolysisMethylAcetate.name: Hydrolysis of Methyl Acetate
hydrolysisMethylAcetate.summary: Under acid or base catalysis, an ester reacts with water and breaks back down into its original carboxylic acid and alcohol — the reverse of esterification.
hydrolysisMethylAcetate.whatChanges: The carbon-oxygen bond within the ester linkage (-COO-) breaks as water is incorporated, regenerating the carboxyl and hydroxyl groups.
hydrolysisMethylAcetate.keyTakeaway: Base-catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) yields the carboxylate salt directly rather than the free acid — the chemistry behind soap-making.

amidationAceticAcidAmmonia.name: Amidation of Acetic Acid and Ammonia
amidationAceticAcidAmmonia.summary: A carboxylic acid and ammonia (or an amine) undergo amidation under heat, releasing one water molecule to form an amide.
amidationAceticAcidAmmonia.whatChanges: A carbon-oxygen bond of the carboxyl group and a nitrogen-hydrogen bond of ammonia break and recombine, forming a new carbon-nitrogen bond and releasing one water molecule.
amidationAceticAcidAmmonia.keyTakeaway: The amide bond is chemically identical to the peptide bond in proteins — this reaction is a key starting point for understanding biological macromolecules.

substitutionMethaneChlorine.name: Free-Radical Substitution of Methane and Chlorine
substitutionMethaneChlorine.summary: Under UV light, methane undergoes free-radical substitution with chlorine gas — a hydrogen atom is replaced by a chlorine atom, and hydrogen chloride is produced as a byproduct.
substitutionMethaneChlorine.whatChanges: Light homolytically breaks the carbon-hydrogen and chlorine-chlorine bonds into radicals, which recombine to form a new carbon-chlorine bond and a new hydrogen-chlorine bond.
substitutionMethaneChlorine.keyTakeaway: This is one of the few reactions alkanes readily undergo, and a classic teaching example of a free-radical mechanism.

q1.question: Which element does the symbol "Na" represent?
q1.explanation: Na is the symbol for Sodium, from the Latin "Natrium".

q2.question: Which element does the symbol "O" represent?
q2.explanation: O is the symbol for Oxygen; Gold, Osmium, and Argon are Au, Os, and Ar.

q3.question: What state of matter is chlorine (Cl) at room temperature?
q3.explanation: Chlorine is a gas at room temperature and pressure, which is why it reacts as Cl₂ gas.

q4.question: Which of these belongs to the "halogen" category?
q4.explanation: Chlorine (Cl) is in group 17, a halogen; sodium is an alkali metal, calcium an alkaline earth metal, iron a transition metal.

q5.question: What state of matter is mercury (Hg) at room temperature?
q5.explanation: Mercury is the only metallic element that is liquid at room temperature and pressure.

q1.question: What is the atomic number of sodium (Na)?
q1.explanation: Sodium's atomic number is 11 — its nucleus has 11 protons.

q2.question: Which of these elements has the highest Pauling electronegativity?
q2.explanation: Oxygen's electronegativity is about 3.44, the highest of these four (H≈2.2, C≈2.55, Na≈0.93).

q3.question: What is the electron configuration of carbon (C)?
q3.explanation: Carbon's electron configuration is [He] 2s² 2p², totaling 6 electrons.

q4.question: Which period of the periodic table is magnesium (Mg) in?
q4.explanation: Magnesium's configuration is [Ne] 3s², placing it in period 3.

q5.question: Which of these elements is an "alkaline earth metal"?
q5.explanation: Calcium is in group 2, an alkaline earth metal; potassium is an alkali metal, aluminium a post-transition metal, silicon a metalloid.

q1.question: Which oxidation state pair is most common for iron (Fe)?
q1.explanation: Iron's most common oxidation states are +2 (ferrous) and +3 (ferric).

q2.question: Which of these elements is a "lanthanide"?
q2.explanation: Cerium (Ce) is a lanthanide; scandium, yttrium, and zirconium are all transition metals.

q3.question: Chromium (Cr) is a well-known "Aufbau exception" — what is its actual electron configuration?
q3.explanation: Chromium's actual configuration is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, favoring a stable half-filled 3d subshell over the [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s² predicted by the general rule.

q4.question: Which category does tungsten (W) belong to?
q4.explanation: Tungsten's d subshell is still being filled, placing it among the transition metals.

q5.question: Which superheavy elements' data is considered "theoretical prediction" rather than fully experimentally verified?
q5.explanation: Elements past #104 are extremely unstable and produced in tiny quantities, so their configurations and oxidation states are mostly theoretical predictions based on periodic trends, not full experimental verification.

q1.question: In the electron configuration "[Ne] 3s¹", what does "[Ne]" represent?
q1.explanation: The bracketed noble-gas symbol is shorthand meaning the element's inner electrons match that noble gas's full configuration exactly.

q2.question: How many valence electrons does a sodium atom (configuration [Ne] 3s¹) have?
q2.explanation: 3s¹ means only 1 outermost electron — why sodium readily loses one electron to form Na⁺.

q3.question: Which category does argon (Ar) belong to?
q3.explanation: Argon's configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶ is a stable octet, making it a noble gas.

q4.question: In oxygen's electron configuration "[He] 2s² 2p⁴", how many electrons are in the 2p subshell?
q4.explanation: The superscript 4 in "2p⁴" means 4 electrons occupy the 2p subshell.

q5.question: Which of these is a "metalloid" element?
q5.explanation: Silicon has properties partway between metals and nonmetals, making it a metalloid — widely used in semiconductors.

q1.question: What type of bond forms between sodium and chlorine in NaCl?
q1.explanation: Sodium transfers a valence electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together by electrostatic attraction — an ionic bond.

q2.question: What type of bond forms between the two hydrogen atoms in H₂?
q2.explanation: Both hydrogen atoms have identical electronegativity, so the shared electron pair is distributed evenly — a nonpolar covalent bond.

q3.question: What type of bond is the O–H bond in a water molecule (H₂O)?
q3.explanation: The electronegativity difference between O and H is about 1.24 (between 0.4 and 1.7), so the shared pair is skewed toward oxygen — a polar covalent bond.

q4.question: What type of bond holds an iron (Fe) lattice together?
q4.explanation: Iron atoms form a lattice of positive ions held together by freely moving valence electrons (an "electron sea") — a metallic bond.

q5.question: What is the weaker attraction between water molecules (H₂O⋯H₂O) called?
q5.explanation: The partially positive hydrogen on one water molecule attracts the partially negative oxygen on another, forming a hydrogen bond.

q1.question: Sodium's electronegativity is about 0.93 and chlorine's is about 3.16. What is their electronegativity difference (ΔEN)?

q2.question: By standard textbook criteria, a bond with ΔEN ≥ 1.7 is usually classified as?
q2.explanation: ΔEN ≥ 1.7 means a very large electronegativity gap — the electron is essentially fully transferred, classifying it as ionic.

q3.question: Hydrogen and chlorine have electronegativities of about 2.2 and 3.16. What is HCl's ΔEN and classification?
q3.explanation: 3.16 − 2.2 = 0.96, which falls between 0.4–1.7, classifying it as polar covalent.

q4.question: When two atoms' electronegativity difference ΔEN < 0.4, the bond is classified as?
q4.explanation: A very small electronegativity difference means the electrons are distributed nearly evenly — nonpolar covalent.

q5.question: Carbon and hydrogen have electronegativities of 2.55 and 2.2 (ΔEN≈0.35). How should the C–H bond in methane (CH₄) be classified?
q5.explanation: 0.35 is below the 0.4 threshold, so the C–H bond is classified as nonpolar covalent.

q1.question: The model describing freely mobile valence electrons in a metallic bond is commonly called?
q1.explanation: Metallic bonding is commonly described with the "electron sea model": positive ions arranged in a lattice, with valence electrons moving freely among them.

q2.question: Why can water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, but CH₄ molecules cannot?
options: Water contains highly electronegative oxygen directly bonded to hydrogen, forming a strongly polarized O–H bond
q2.explanation: Hydrogen bonding requires hydrogen bonded directly to a highly electronegative atom (O, N, or F); carbon in CH₄ isn't electronegative enough and lacks this strongly polarized bond, so no hydrogen bonding occurs.

q3.question: Which statement about hydrogen bonds is correct?
options: Hydrogen bonds are stronger than typical covalent bonds
A hydrogen bond is an intermolecular force, weaker than a covalent bond
Hydrogen bonds only exist in metals
Hydrogen bonds have nothing to do with electronegativity
q3.explanation: Hydrogen bonds are intermolecular forces — stronger than van der Waals forces, but still clearly weaker than covalent bonds.

q4.question: Under the electronegativity-difference classification, what happens when ΔEN is exactly 1.7?
q4.explanation: The rule classifies ΔEN ≥ 1.7 as ionic, so a value of exactly 1.7 is still classified as ionic.

q5.question: In a metallic lattice (like Fe), what is the main role of the free electrons?
options: Fixed in place on specific atoms
Moving freely among the positive ions, the basis of conductivity and malleability
q5.explanation: Metals' electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, and malleability all stem from these valence electrons moving freely among the positive ions.

q1.question: What is the molecular shape of carbon dioxide (CO₂)?
q1.explanation: CO₂'s two C=O bonds are arranged at 180°, making it a linear molecule.

q2.question: What is the molecular shape of a water molecule (H₂O)?
q2.explanation: Two lone pairs on the oxygen compress the bond angle, giving H₂O a bent shape (about 104.5°).

q3.question: What is the molecular shape of ammonia (NH₃)?
q3.explanation: A lone pair on the nitrogen gives NH₃ a trigonal pyramidal shape.

q4.question: What is the molecular shape of methane (CH₄)?
q4.explanation: Carbon's sp³ hybridized orbitals bond symmetrically to 4 hydrogens, forming a regular tetrahedron.

q5.question: How many atoms does one water molecule (H₂O) contain in total?
q5.explanation: H₂O consists of 1 oxygen atom and 2 hydrogen atoms — 3 atoms total.

q1.question: Why is a water molecule (H₂O) polar, even though it's made only of polar O–H bonds?
options: Because it contains an ionic bond
Because its bent shape prevents the bond dipoles from cancelling out
Because the oxygen atom is positively charged
Because it contains a metallic bond
q1.explanation: The bent structure makes the two O–H bond dipoles asymmetric, so the net dipole moment isn't zero — making the molecule polar overall.

q2.question: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) contains polar C=O bonds, yet the molecule overall is nonpolar. Why?
options: The molecule is linear and symmetric, so the bond dipoles cancel out
q2.explanation: The two equal-and-opposite C=O bond dipoles cancel out exactly in the linear structure, giving a net dipole moment of zero.

q3.question: What molecular geometry is benzene (C₆H₆) classified as?
q3.explanation: All 6 carbon atoms and 6 hydrogen atoms of the benzene ring lie in the same plane — a planar structure.

q4.question: Which of these molecules is "nonpolar"?
q4.explanation: CH₄'s symmetric tetrahedral shape makes its four C–H bond dipoles cancel out, making it nonpolar.

q5.question: What is NaCl's molecular geometry classified as?
q5.explanation: NaCl doesn't form a fixed covalent geometry — it's represented as an ionic pair held together by electrostatic attraction.

q1.question: The functional group "-OH" is called?
q1.explanation: "-OH" is the hydroxyl group, commonly found in alcohols.

q2.question: The functional group "-COOH" is called?
q2.explanation: "-COOH" is the carboxyl group, the signature functional group of carboxylic acids.

q3.question: Which functional group does ethanol contain?
q3.explanation: Ethanol contains one -OH group, the hydroxyl functional group characteristic of alcohols.

q4.question: Which functional groups does acetic acid (CH₃COOH) contain?
q4.explanation: The carboxyl group (-COOH) itself contains a carbonyl (C=O), so acetic acid is classified as having both carboxyl and carbonyl groups.

q5.question: The functional group "C=C" is called?
q5.explanation: A carbon-carbon double bond "C=C" is the signature structure of an alkene.

q1.question: Which organic category does benzene belong to?
q1.explanation: Benzene's distinctive cyclic conjugated structure earns it its own "aromatic" category.

q2.question: According to the reaction relationship graph, what can an alcohol's "oxidation" reaction ultimately produce?
options: An aldehyde/ketone, which can be further oxidized to a carboxylic acid
q2.explanation: Oxidizing an alcohol first produces an aldehyde or ketone (depending on the alcohol type), and an aldehyde can be further oxidized into a carboxylic acid.

q3.question: According to the reaction relationship graph, what does a carboxylic acid + alcohol "esterification" reaction produce?
q3.explanation: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol undergo acid-catalyzed esterification to produce an ester and water.

q4.question: What does an ester convert back into via "hydrolysis"?
q4.explanation: Hydrolysis is the reverse of esterification: an ester reacting with water produces a carboxylic acid (and an alcohol).

q5.question: What does acetylene (C₂H₂) first produce via "hydrogenation"?
q5.explanation: Hydrogenating an alkyne first produces an alkene (acetylene → ethylene); only further hydrogenation produces an alkane (ethylene → ethane).

q1.question: What are the products of methane's (CH₄) combustion reaction?
q1.explanation: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces carbon dioxide and water.

q2.question: What does ethylene produce when hydrogenated with H₂ over a Ni catalyst with heating?
q2.explanation: Hydrogenating ethylene's carbon-carbon double bond turns it into a single bond, producing ethane.

q3.question: What does ethylene produce when reacted with water (H₂O) via "addition", catalyzed by acid (H₃PO₄) with heating?
q3.explanation: Water adds across ethylene's double bond to produce ethanol — one industrial method for manufacturing ethanol.

q4.question: What reaction condition does methane's combustion require?
q4.explanation: Combustion requires ignition to start, after which it continues releasing heat on its own.

q5.question: Which catalyst is used to hydrogenate acetylene into ethylene?
q5.explanation: The Lindlar catalyst stops hydrogenation at the alkene stage, preventing further hydrogenation to an alkane.

q1.question: What oxidizing agent is used to oxidize ethanol into acetaldehyde?
q1.explanation: This reaction uses potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇) under acidic conditions as the oxidizing agent.

q2.question: What oxidizing agent further oxidizes acetaldehyde into acetic acid?
q2.explanation: This step uses potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) under acidic conditions to fully oxidize the aldehyde into a carboxylic acid.

q3.question: What does the "condensation" of two methanol molecules under concentrated sulfuric acid and heat produce?
q3.explanation: Two methanol molecules condense (losing water) to form dimethyl ether (an ether) and water.

q4.question: Acetic acid and methanol undergo esterification to form methyl acetate. What is its "reverse reaction"?
q4.explanation: Esterification and hydrolysis are reverse reactions of each other: esterification produces an ester and water, while hydrolysis reacts an ester with water back into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.

q5.question: What are the products of methane reacting with chlorine (Cl₂) via substitution under UV light?
q5.explanation: UV light provides the energy to homolytically split Cl₂ into radicals, which substitute one hydrogen on methane to produce chloromethane and HCl.

q1.question: Which of these elements has the highest electronegativity?
q1.explanation: Fluorine's electronegativity is about 3.98 — the highest of any known element.

q2.question: Which of these molecules has a "tetrahedral" shape?
q2.explanation: CH₄'s carbon uses sp³ hybridized orbitals to bond symmetrically to 4 hydrogens, forming a tetrahedron; H₂O is bent, NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal, and CO₂ is linear.

q3.question: What kind of functional group can an alcohol's oxidation reaction produce?
q3.explanation: The first step of alcohol oxidation produces an aldehyde or ketone, both containing a carbonyl group.

q4.question: What is the reaction type of methane's combustion reaction called?
q4.explanation: Combustion is technically a form of oxidation, but MoleculeOS's reaction data lists it as its own "combustion" type.

q5.question: Lanthanides and actinides are conventionally shown in their own row below the main periodic table because their "group" field is?
q5.explanation: Lanthanides and actinides don't map cleanly onto the main table's 1–18 group columns, so they're stored as group=null and conventionally shown as two separate rows.

electronegativity.definition: An atom's ability to attract shared electrons in a bond; a higher value means a stronger pull, usually expressed on the Pauling scale.

vsepr.definition: Predicts a molecule's 3D shape from the repulsion between electron domains around the central atom.

lonePair.definition: A pair of valence electrons on the central atom that isn't involved in bonding; usually affects molecular shape more than bonding pairs do.

polarCovalentBond.definition: A bond where unequal electronegativity pulls the shared electron pair toward one atom, creating partial charges (δ+ / δ-).

functionalGroup.definition: A specific group of atoms in a molecule that determines its main chemical properties, e.g. -OH (hydroxyl), -COOH (carboxyl).

delocalizedElectron.definition: An electron not confined to a single atom or bond, free to spread across several atoms — common in metallic bonding and benzene's conjugated ring.

hydrogenBond.definition: A relatively strong intermolecular force between hydrogen and a small, highly electronegative atom (O, N, F).

hydrolysis.definition: The reaction of an ester with water to form a carboxylic acid and an alcohol — the reverse of esterification.

waterBentShape.title: Why is H₂O a bent shape?
waterBentShape.explain: The oxygen at the center of a water molecule has 4 electron domains: 2 bonding pairs (to each hydrogen) and 2 lone pairs. Per VSEPR theory, all 4 domains push as far apart as possible, giving a tetrahedral arrangement of electron domains — but molecular shape only counts atom positions, and lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing the H-O-H angle from the ideal 109.5° down to about 104.5°. That's why H₂O is bent rather than linear.
socratic: How many total electron domains (bonding plus lone pairs) does the central oxygen have?
If there were no lone pairs, what shape would 4 electron domains form?
Which repels more strongly, a lone pair or a bonding pair — and how does that change the bond angle?
waterBentShape.hint: Start by counting the bonding pairs and lone pairs around the oxygen.

polarityCheck.title: How do I tell whether a molecule is polar?
polarityCheck.explain: Two steps: first, check bond polarity — the bigger the electronegativity difference between two atoms, the more polar the bond. Second, check whether the molecule's shape is symmetric — even if every bond is polar, if the geometry makes the individual bond dipoles cancel out (like linear CO₂), the molecule as a whole can still be nonpolar; a bent molecule like H₂O can't cancel its bond dipoles, so it stays polar.
socratic: How large is the electronegativity difference across each bond in this molecule?
Is the molecule's geometry symmetric enough that the bond dipoles would cancel out?
polarityCheck.hint: Having polar bonds isn't enough on its own — check whether the shape is symmetric too.

ionicVsCovalent.title: What's the difference between an ionic bond and a covalent bond?
ionicVsCovalent.explain: Ionic bonds form between atoms with a large electronegativity difference (usually a metal and a nonmetal): electrons are fully transferred, forming ions that then attract each other electrostatically, e.g. NaCl. Covalent bonds form between nonmetals, where atoms share one or more electron pairs, e.g. H₂ or CH₄. Rule of thumb: a larger electronegativity difference skews more ionic; a small or zero difference skews covalent.
socratic: Are the two atoms metals or nonmetals?
Roughly how large is their electronegativity difference?
Are the electrons being transferred or shared?
ionicVsCovalent.hint: First check whether each atom is a metal or nonmetal, then compare electronegativity.

electronegativityTrend.title: What's the electronegativity trend across the periodic table?
electronegativityTrend.explain: Electronegativity describes how strongly an atom pulls on a shared electron pair. Across the periodic table, it generally increases going up a group and increases going right across a period, which is why fluorine (F) is the most electronegative element and alkali metals (Na, K) are among the least. A larger electronegativity difference between two atoms skews the bond more ionic; a small difference skews it more covalent.
socratic: Going left to right and bottom to top on the periodic table, does electronegativity generally increase or decrease?
Roughly where on the periodic table are the highest and lowest electronegativity elements?
electronegativityTrend.hint: Remember the general rule: electronegativity is highest toward the upper right (excluding noble gases).

hydrogenBondingWater.title: Why is water's boiling point higher than expected?
hydrogenBondingWater.explain: A hydrogen bond is a relatively strong intermolecular force between a hydrogen atom and a small, highly electronegative atom (O, N, F): once hydrogen forms a polar covalent bond with one of these atoms, its partial positive charge is attracted to a lone pair's partial negative charge on a neighboring molecule. Water molecules form extensive hydrogen bonds with each other, which raises water's boiling point far above what its molecular weight alone would predict, and gives solid ice an open lattice that's less dense than liquid water — which is why ice floats.
socratic: Hydrogen bonds typically form between hydrogen and which highly electronegative atoms?
Would water's boiling point still be this high without hydrogen bonding?
hydrogenBondingWater.hint: Think about which atom in water carries a partial negative charge, and which hydrogen carries a partial positive charge.

metallicBonding.title: How does metallic bonding form?
metallicBonding.explain: Metallic bonding can be pictured as positively charged metal cations sitting in a 'sea' of freely moving electrons — a metal's valence electrons don't belong to any single atom, but move freely through the whole lattice. This electron sea is why metals conduct electricity and heat, and why they can bend and stretch without breaking (the cations can slide and rearrange while the electron sea keeps surrounding them).
socratic: In metallic bonding, do the electrons belong to one specific atom, or can they move freely?
Why does this bonding style explain both conductivity and malleability?
metallicBonding.hint: Key terms: delocalized electrons, electron sea.

alcoholReactions.title: What reactions can alcohols undergo?
alcoholReactions.explain: An alcohol's defining functional group is the hydroxyl (-OH). Per MoleculeOS's reaction map, an alcohol can be oxidized into a carbonyl-containing aldehyde or ketone (an aldehyde can then be further oxidized into a carboxylic acid), react with a carboxylic acid via esterification to form an ester plus water, or undergo condensation with another alcohol to form an ether. Ethanol is the most common representative alcohol.
socratic: What is an alcohol's functional group?
What functional group can an alcohol's oxidation product become first?
alcoholReactions.hint: Locate the -OH group first — its position affects what the oxidation product will be.

esterification.title: How does esterification happen?
esterification.explain: Esterification is the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol, catalyzed by acid (typically concentrated sulfuric acid) and heat, producing an ester and water. It's reversible — the reverse reaction (ester + water → carboxylic acid + alcohol) is called hydrolysis. For example, acetic acid and methanol esterify to form methyl acetate and water.
steps: Identify the reactants: a carboxylic acid (-COOH) and an alcohol (-OH).
Under acid catalysis (e.g. concentrated sulfuric acid) and heat, the acid's -OH and the alcohol's H leave as a water molecule.
The products are an ester and water; the reaction is reversible, and its reverse is hydrolysis.
socratic: What two functional groups does esterification need as reactants?
What catalyst and conditions does this reaction need, and what's its reverse reaction called?
esterification.hint: Rule of thumb: acid + alcohol → ester + water, and the reverse is hydrolysis.

combustionMethane.title: How do you write methane's combustion equation?
combustionMethane.explain: Methane (CH₄) burns completely in excess oxygen to produce carbon dioxide, water, and a large amount of heat: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. This is the chemical basis of natural gas as a fuel; the reaction needs ignition to start, and then keeps releasing heat on its own.
steps: Write the reactants: CH₄ and O₂.
Identify the complete-combustion products: CO₂ and H₂O.
socratic: What are the two products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
When balancing this equation, which element is easiest to balance first?
combustionMethane.hint: Balance carbon first, then hydrogen, then oxygen.

aromaticBenzene.title: Why is benzene classified separately as aromatic?
aromaticBenzene.explain: Benzene (C₆H₆) has six carbons arranged in a ring with electrons delocalized across the whole conjugated system. This gives it distinct stability and chemistry compared to ordinary alkenes, so MoleculeOS's organic classification lists it separately as 'aromatic' rather than grouping it with alkenes.
socratic: Are benzene's ring electrons concentrated in a few specific bonds, or spread across the whole ring?
Why does this structure make benzene especially stable?
aromaticBenzene.hint: Key terms: delocalized electrons, conjugated ring, aromaticity.

additionHydrogenation.title: How does hydrogenation (an addition reaction) work?
additionHydrogenation.explain: Hydrogenation is an addition reaction: hydrogen gas (H₂), with a metal catalyst (e.g. Ni), adds across a carbon-carbon double or triple bond, turning it into a single bond. Ethylene hydrogenates into ethane, for example; for a triple bond (acetylene), a special Lindlar catalyst (Pd/CaCO₃) is used to stop the reaction at the alkene stage instead of continuing all the way to an alkane.
steps: Confirm the starting molecule has a carbon-carbon double or triple bond (unsaturated).
Choose the right catalyst: Ni for full hydrogenation; a Lindlar catalyst to stop a triple bond at the alkene stage.
H₂ adds across the double/triple bond, reducing bond order and increasing hydrogen count.
socratic: What kind of catalyst does hydrogenation need?
If you start from a triple bond (an alkyne), how do you stop the reaction at the alkene stage instead of going all the way to an alkane?
additionHydrogenation.hint: A regular catalyst hydrogenates all the way to an alkane; a Lindlar catalyst stops at the alkene.

amideAmine.title: What's the difference between an amine and an amide?
amideAmine.explain: An amine's functional group is an amino group (-NH₂ or a derivative), which you can picture as ammonia (NH₃) with one or more hydrogens replaced by a carbon chain. An amide is the product of a carboxylic acid reacting with ammonia (or an amine), containing an amide group — for example, acetic acid reacting with ammonia produces acetamide. The amide bond is also how amino acids link together in proteins.
socratic: What atoms make up the amino group versus the amide group?
An amide is formed from which two functional groups or molecules reacting?
amideAmine.hint: Amide = carboxylic acid + ammonia (or an amine), after they react.
